- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is positive or neutral (sentiment > 0.5) — model tends to overshoot and fail to correct.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is negative or weak (sentiment < 0.3) — model fails to recognize downward pressure or mean reversion.
- Model exhibits persistent lag in responding to sentiment shifts — especially when sentiment turns negative, forecast remains high for 2–3 days.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed (e.g., alternating 0.3–0.7), model overfits recent highs and underreacts to mean reversion.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overweights recent price momentum, ignoring longer-term mean reversion signals — especially when sentiment is low or flat.
- If sentiment is consistently low (e.g., < 0.2) over last 5 days, reduce forecast by 5–10% to account for downward bias.
- If sentiment is consistently high (e.g., > 0.8) over last 5 days, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overconfidence in upward momentum.
- Model tends to overcorrect after sharp declines — forecasts rebound too quickly, missing the true mean reversion path.
- When sentiment is near zero (0.0–0.3), forecast should be anchored to 3–5 day moving average, not recent peak.
